 Futura Team 
 Pia Gray 
 For generations, extreme weather, landmines, and decades of civil war left Angola’s Lisima plateau largely unexamined by modern scientists, a dynamic that shifted in February 2026, when conservation ecologist Rob Taylor led a sixteen-member international team into the high-altitude wetlands over the rainy season. Working through flooded peatlands that feed four major African river basins, the team documented over 70 candidate species that could be new to science. 
 Organized by The Wilderness Project under the Cassai Life Atlas initiative, the expedition brought together African and international specialists to map the upper Cassai catchment area in Moxico Province . Their findings demonstrate how much biodiversity remains uncataloged across the high-altitude wetlands of the Angolan Highlands Water Tower .

 Navigating mud, malaria, and uncharted terrain
 Reaching the Lisima plateau required crossing some of the most difficult terrain in southern Africa. Heavy rains turned dirt tracks into swamps, frequently stranding the team’s convoy in mud for an entire day at a time.
 The team faced vehicle breakdowns and several cases of malaria along the route, supported by landmine clearance crews from The HALO Trust and local experts from Fundação Lisima . When travel stalled, the team explored nearby dambos—seasonally flooded grasslands—and isolated swamp forests that had never been documented by biologists.
 This fieldwork builds on more than a decade of earlier research across the Okavango and Lungwevungu headwaters. Those previous surveys confirmed over 70 species new to science, laying the groundwork for this latest push into the Cassai basin.
 High counts across dragonflies, moths, and crickets
 Field surveys revealed an impressive array of insect life across the plateau’s riverbanks and grasslands. The team cataloged 103 dragonfly and damselfly species, including 34 new to the Lisima region, six added to Angola’s national list, and eight undescribed species now undergoing formal study.
 Researchers also documented 47 distinct species of grasshoppers, katydids, and crickets, identifying three candidate species that appear new to science. These records significantly expand what biologists know about insect distribution across central Africa.
 The team also found a wide variety of moths and butterflies,with over 1,000 species recorded during the trip. By collecting and rearing caterpillars, the team linked 25 geometer moth species to 19 host plants, estimating that up to six percent of all moth species observed on the expedition may have been unknown to science.
 Fluorescent spiders and unconfirmed laboratory finds
 Among the night discoveries was an undescribed crowned crab spider , provisionally labeled Smodicinus sp. nov., which glows bright blue under ultraviolet light. While the glowing trait drew attention, researchers stress that the underlying chemical mechanism and biological purpose of the fluorescence remain unknown.
 The team also collected a ladybird orb-web spider, identified as Paraplectana sp. nov., alongside several unusual beetle and scorpion specimens. Biologists emphasize that “new to science” remains a provisional label until laboratory examinations are complete.
 Under international rules of zoological nomenclature, a species becomes formally recognized only after taxonomists compare preserved specimens against existing collections and publish detailed peer-reviewed descriptions.
 Establishing an ecological reference for the future
 The Cassai Life Atlas survey provides researchers with their first detailed ecological record for the Lisima plateau. Taxonomists expect the formal verification process for all candidate species to take months or years of thorough laboratory work.
 Beyond individual species discoveries, the expedition establishes a critical benchmark for a region whose rivers feed the Congo, Okavango, Zambezi, and Cuanza basins. Having a clear record of local wildlife allows conservationists to track habitat changes and design targeted protection measures for Angola’s headwaters.
 Source: The Wilderness Project, “Dozens of New Species Discovered in Angola,” Cassai Life Atlas announcement, June 2, 2026.
